title: A Real-Time Dynamic Study on the Synergistic Effects of Grain Size and Cooling Rate on Intragranular Ferrite Formation in Steels
abstract: Abstract Precise control of non-metallic inclusions is essential for achieving the desired mechanical properties of steels. Generally, fine inclusions are relatively difficult to remove completely during the refining process. They can serve as the heterogeneous nucleation sites for the formation of intragranular ferrite (IGF). This interlocked microstructure is the preferred type in the coarse-grain heat-affected zone of weldments to improve the toughness at low temperatures. In this study, two representative grades of low-alloy steels with 0.2 and 0.4 pct carbon were used to investigate the synergistic influence of the prior austenite grain size (PAGS) and cooling rate on IGF formation.  In-situ  observation experiments using high-temperature confocal laser scanning microscope, thermodynamic calculations and electron microscopy characterizations were used to investigate this synergistic effect in the two steel grades. It is found that the coarse grains can promote IGF nucleation and growth at an intermediate cooling rate, while smaller grain size requires a higher cooling rate as a driving force for IGF formation. This synergistic effect was verified in the steels with 0.2 and 0.4 pct carbon. The current work provides a quantitative study on the comprehensive influence of PAGS and cooling rate on IGF formation. The obtained findings are validated for general low-alloy steels with different carbon contents, contributing to the development of the ‘Oxide Metallurgy’ concept.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Non-metallic inclusions are generally considered to be detrimental to the mechanical properties of steels, particularly degrading toughness and fatigue resistance. [ 1 ]  The complete removal of fine inclusions remains complex and costly. Considering this situation, a concept of ‘oxide metallurgy (OM)’ has been introduced as a potential solution. Oxide metallurgy (OM) technology [ 2 ]  utilizes finely dispersed inclusions in steel to exert two principal effects,  i.e.,  pinning austenite grain growth and facilitating the formation of complex inclusions that induce IGF nucleation during cooling. IGF nucleates heterogeneously on the surface of specific types of inclusions and grows radially, forming a fine, plate-like, and highly interlocked microstructure. This interlocked arrangement of IGF laths subdivides the prior austenite grain and can effectively hinder crack propagation, significantly enhancing the low-temperature toughness and resistance to brittle fracture. Particularly, this OM technology is applied in the weld heat-affected zone (HAZ) of low-alloy steels. [ 3 ]

Several factors influence IGF nucleation and growth on the surface of non-metallic inclusions, including the chemical composition, size, and number density of inclusions, [ 4 ]  cooling rate from 800 to 500 °C, [ 5 ]  and prior austenite grain size (PAGS). [ 6 ]  For instance, TiO inclusion is highly effective in promoting intragranular ferrite (IGF) formation due to its low lattice misfit with the ferrite phase. Previous research has demonstrated that Ti-oxides can provide optimal nucleation sites among oxides, as their lattice aligns favorably with the growing ferrite phase. [ 7 ]  In contrast, more complex inclusions, such as TiN and MnS, exhibit reduced nucleation potency for IGF. This is primarily due to their larger lattice misfit with the ferrite phase. [ 8 ]  Similarly, MnS inclusions, which are commonly found in many steels, are less effective in nucleating IGF due to their inability to form stable nucleation sites. [ 9 ]  The size and distribution of inclusions play a critical role in IGF nucleation. Grong  et al. [ 10 ]  suggested that the optimal size for nucleating inclusions is around 1  µ m. Inclusions larger than 2  µ m can act as crack initiators, leading to a degradation of steel mechanical properties. The inclusions with a size of smaller than 0.5  µ m may lack the necessary capacity to induce IGF nucleation. Therefore, inclusions in a range of 0.5–1  µ m are most effective in promoting fine, interlocked IGF structures that enhance crack resistance and improve toughness. Additionally, Loder  et al. [ 11 ]  emphasized that the number of specific kinds of inclusions should be sufficiently high to provide an adequate number of nucleation sites but should be kept as low as possible to meet the cleanliness requirements of high-quality steels.

As one of the key factors controlling the final microstructure, the cooling rate can play a critical role in inclusion-induced IGF nucleation and growth. From the viewpoint of phase transformation kinetics, the cooling rate controls the undercooling and the diffusion time of solute elements. It also changes the transformation path from austenite to ferrite, thereby affecting the nucleation rate and area fraction of IGF. [ 12 ]  Li  et al. [ 13 ]  performed continuous-cooling experiments on a rare-earth La-deoxidised steel. The study found that stable IGF can be obtained at cooling rates of 4 to 10 °C/s, with the most developed IGF observed at about 8 °C/s. Yang  et al. [ 14 ]  carried out  in-situ  high-temperature observations at different cooling rates in a Ti-Zr deoxidized steel. Their study showed that the IGF volume fraction first increases and then decreases with increasing cooling rate. They also found that the cooling rate has little effect on the inclusion type but can significantly refine the inclusion size, thereby enhancing the nucleation potency of fine inclusions for IGF. In addition to the cooling rate, the prior austenite grain size has a pronounced effect on IGF formation. Wan  et al. [ 15 ]  investigated the austenite to IGF transformation behavior in a simulated coarse-grain heat-affected zone (CGHAZ) of a high-strength low-alloy steel. They reported that IGF preferentially forms inside coarse austenite grains, whereas finer grains are mainly occupied by bainite. Zhang  et al. [ 16 ]  systematically examined the effect of austenite grain size on IGF formation in a C-Mn steel. Their results showed that the nucleation of grain boundary ferrite is significantly suppressed as the austenite grain size increases. In this case, Ti-rich inclusions become the preferred heterogeneous nucleation sites for IGF. To provide an overview of this research area, Table  I  summarizes the current studies on the effects of cooling rate and PAGS on IGF formation in steels. Previous investigations have primarily examined the effects of cooling rate and PAGS on IGF formation in isolation. However, in actual casting and welding processes, these two factors jointly influence IGF nucleation and growth. Based on this, the present study quantitatively investigates the synergistic mechanism of cooling rate and PAGS on IGF formation. The conventional low-alloy steels with a wide range of carbon contents from 0.2 to 0.4 pct are used as the alloy composition to verify the findings.

sections.heading: Experimental Methods
paragraphs: The chemical compositions of the Fe-0.2 pct C and Fe-0.4 pct C alloys are listed in Table  II . Specimens were cut into 4 × 4 × 1.5 mm plates and mirror-polished by sequential grinding with 320#, 600#, and 1200# SiC papers, followed by polishing with 3 and 1  µ m diamond suspensions.  In-situ  observation experiments were performed using high-temperature confocal laser scanning microscope (HT-CLSM). Previous studies have shown that the CGHAZ is dominated by a higher peak temperature. The peak temperature is typically in the range of 1350 °C to 1400 °C. [ 25 ]  In contrast, the FGHAZ experiences a lower peak temperature. A peak temperature of 1200 °C lies close to the boundary between the FGHAZ and the CGHAZ. [ 26 ]  Therefore, 1400 °C and 1200 °C were selected in this work to simulate the typical conditions of the CGHAZ and FGHAZ, respectively. Figure  1  shows the thermal profile employed. Specimens were first heated to 423 K (150 °C) at 40 °C/min and held for 120 seconds. They were then heated to 1273 K (1000 °C) at 100 °C/min without holding. Finally, they were heated at 150 °C/min to either 1473 K (1200 °C) or 1673 K (1400 °C), where they were held for 120 seconds. Two peak temperatures,  i.e.,  1473 K (1200 °C) and 1673 K (1400 °C) were thus employed to control the size of PAGS. Huda  et al. [ 27 ]  used cooling rates of 2, 5, and 10 °C/s in CGHAZ thermal simulations. Liu  et al. [ 28 ]  used 1, 10, and 30 °C/s in Gleeble simulations of the ICR-CGHAZ. Based on these previous studies, we selected 70, 300, and 600 °C/min as three cooling rates in this work. They correspond to approximately 1.17, 5, and 10 °C/s, respectively. This range represents slow, intermediate, and fast-cooling severities relevant to practical CGHAZ welding thermal cycles. Table II Chemical Compositions of the Materials Used in This Study (Mass Percentage, Wt Pct) Sample C Si Mn Al Ti O N S Fe Sample A 0.227 0.38 0.91 0.002 0.008 0.0071 0.029 0.009 bal. Sample B 0.374 0.31 1.33 0.002 0.01 0.0057 0.020 0.009 bal. Fig. 1 Schematic diagram of  in-situ  heating and cooling cycle in this study

High-purity Ar (purity > 99.999 pct) was cleaned by passing the gas through a gas cleaning system to remove moisture and impurity gases. Before heating the sample, the chamber of HT-CLSM was filled with pure Ar under a flow of 50 mL/min and subsequently evacuated to desorb the remaining air. The cycle of vacuum and purging with Ar was performed three times to clean the chamber thoroughly. The sample was located inside Al 2 O 3  crucibles with a 4.5 mm inner diameter. Temperature at the crucible bottom was monitored by a Type-R thermocouple (TC); the sample surface temperature has been reported to be approximately 25 °C lower than the TC reading. [ 5 ]

Elemental analysis was performed using energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer (EDS) measurements on a JEOL JSM-7800F field emission gun scanning electron microscope (FEG-SEM) at 15 kV. After HT-CLSM, specimens were repolished, etched in 4 pct Nital solution, and examined using a scanning electron microscope (SEM). Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was performed on a Zeiss Sigma 300 SEM equipped with an Oxford Nordlys Nano EBSD detector, and data were processed in AztecCrystal. Selected HT-CLSM micrographs analyzed using Image-J were used to quantify the area fractions of IGF and GBF. PAGS was evaluated in ImageJ as the average of 10 representative grains per sample, a validated statistical approach adopted because large grains limited the number of complete grains per cross-section. [ 6 ]  For finer-grained samples, the 10-grain average agreed well with that from 20 grains.

sections.heading: Calculation Methods
Characteristics of Non-metallic Inclusions in Steel
paragraphs: To identify different types of non-metallic inclusions in the Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC alloys, the following analytical approaches were employed. Thermodynamic equilibrium calculations using Thermo-Calc software were performed to predict possible inclusion phases and their formation conditions. Automatic analysis was used to determine the statistical distributions of inclusion elements. Scanning electron microscopy-energy-dispersive spectroscopy (SEM-EDS) was applied to characterize the morphology and chemical composition of inclusions.

Figure  3 (a) shows the thermodynamic calculation results of the formation of stable-phase inclusions in the Fe-0.2pctC alloy. Besides the dominant BCC or face-FCC phases, as the temperature decreases from 1500 °C, LIQUID#2 (liquid inclusions with certain solubility of Mn, Si, Al, Ti, O,  etc. ) and the CORUNDUM phase ((Ti,Al)2O3) remain stable in sequence. When the temperature drops to 1300 °C, the equilibrium-phase combination corresponding to the solidified inclusion composition becomes MnS phase and FCC_A1#2 (TiN) phase. The equilibrium calculation results of inclusion precipitation in the Fe-0.4 pctC alloy are shown in Figure  4 (b). It is found that the inclusion precipitation sequence is almost the same as that of the Fe-0.2 pctC alloy. When the temperature is lower than 1300 °C, the stable phases are LIQUID#2, the MnS phase, FCC_A1#2 (TiN), and the CORUNDUM ((Ti,Al) 2 O 3 ) phase. Fig. 3 Inclusion formation at different temperatures calculated using Thermo-Calc 2024b software and the TCFE13 database, ( a ) Fe-0.2 pctC alloy, ( b ) Fe-0.4 pctC alloy Fig. 4 Inclusion types in the (a) Fe-0.2 pctC and ( b ) Fe-0.4 pctC alloys

Automatic analysis was employed to statistically evaluate the non-metallic inclusions in the two alloys. Figure  4 (a) and (b) illustrate the type distributions of typical inclusions in the Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC alloys. The results indicate that both alloys contain complex inclusions comprising MnS, Al 2 O 3 , and TiN.

Figure  5  illustrates the morphology and elemental distribution of complex inclusions in Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC steels via SEM-EDS analysis. For Fe-0.2 pctC alloy, inclusions typically exhibit a TiN core surrounded by a (Mn, Si, Al, Ti)-O oxide layer. This is consistent with LIQUID#2 or CORUNDUM phases predicted by thermodynamic calculations. In addition, MnS outer shells could be found surrounding the oxide core. A similar composition could be observed in the Fe-0.4 pctC alloy, although some inclusions show TiN located at the MnS periphery. MnS inclusions are generally ineffective as nucleation sites due to their large lattice misfit with IGF and poor coherency with the austenite matrix, resulting in high interfacial energy. [ 31 ]  However, the precipitation of MnS in austenite substantially depletes the Mn solute in the surrounding matrix, forming a manganese-depleted zone (MDZ) around the inclusions, which is recognized as a key factor promoting IGF nucleation. [ 32 ] Fig. 5 SEM-EDS analysis of the chemical element distribution maps of the Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC alloys: ( a ) Fe-0.2 pctC; ( b ) Fe-0.4 pctC

Beyond the composition, inclusion size also influences IGF nucleation obviously. As shown in Figure  7 , most inclusions in both Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC alloys ranging from 0.5 to 2.0  μ m. The Fe-0.2 pctC alloy contains a slightly higher fraction of large inclusions (> 1.0  μ m) and a larger mean size than Fe-0.4 pctC alloy. The nucleation barrier for IGF is lowest for inclusions in the 0.5–1.0  μ m size range, where 65 pct of the inclusions in the Fe-0.2 pctC alloy and 58 pct in the Fe-0.4 pctC alloy are located. In addition, excessively large particles (> 2.0  μ m) tend to act as crack initiation sites, which is detrimental to impact toughness. [ 10 ]  Thus, maintaining inclusion sizes within 0.4-1.1 μm could balance IGF formation and mechanical integrity. [ 35 ] Fig. 7 The distribution of inclusion size in the proposed ( a ) Fe-0.2 pctC and ( b ) Fe-0.4 pctC alloys

sections.heading: Effect of Grain Size on the Nucleation and Growth of IGF
paragraphs: Prior austenite grain size (PAGS) is a key parameter to control IGF formation. Markedly different PAGS were produced by peak heating to 1200 °C and 1400 °C with 120 seconds holds.  In-situ  HT-CLSM observations showed in Figure  8  reveal progressive austenite coarsening driven by grain boundary migration and the coalescence of smaller grains with increasing temperature and holding duration. Table  IV  quantifies that the grain size of Fe-0.2 pctC increases from 27.88  μ m at 1200 °C to 290.27  μ m at 1400 °C, whereas that of Fe-0.4 pctC increases from 33.30 to 349.92  μ m. Coarsening occurs predominantly during the 1400 °C holding stage, yielding a coarse austenite grain structure. Fig. 8 Austenite grain growth process in a Fe-0.2 pctC alloy during heating and isothermal holding: ( a ) 1200 °C; ( b ) 1300 °C; ( c ) 1400 °C; and ( d ) 1400 °C after isothermal holding for 120 s Table IV PAGS of Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC Alloys After Holding at Different Temperatures for 120 s Holding Condition (Temperature × Time) PAGS/ μ m Sample A 1200 °C × 120 s 27.88 ± 5  µ m Sample A 1400 °C × 120 s 290.27 ± 30  µ m Sample B 1200 °C × 120 s 33.30 ± 5  µ m Sample B 1400 °C × 120 s 349.92 ± 30  µ m

Generally, the growth of austenite grains results from the competition between the driving force for grain growth and the forces that hinder grain boundary motion. [ 36 ]  As the maximum heating temperature increases, the retarding effects of solute drag [ 37 ]  and particle pinning [ 38 ]  become less effective, which facilitates grain boundary migration. When the maximum heating temperature exceeds a critical value and the driving force for grain growth surpasses the resistance to grain boundary motion, austenite grains grow rapidly.

Figure  9  illustrates the phase transitions of Fe-0.2 pctC alloy holding at different maximum temperatures, showing that PAGS changes significantly, and this will result in triggering IGF nucleation and growth decisively. This can be confirmed by checking the final microstructure at room temperature. When the steel was held at 1200 °C for 120 seconds and was cooled at 70 °C/min, its microstructure exhibited a minimal transformation and no IGF formation could be observed. This indicates the formation of ferrite with a blocky morphology and small PAGS (≈27.9  µ m). In contrast, for the steel held at 1400 °C for 120 seconds (PAGS ≈290.3  µ m), GBF preferentially nucleated at grain boundaries at 716 °C, followed by IGF nucleation on intragranular inclusions at 691 °C. This phenomenon is termed symbiotic nucleation [ 39 ]  and the temperature of finishing transformation is approximately 600 °C. The results obtained demonstrate that larger austenite grains can promote IGF formation by reducing grain boundary nucleation competition and providing more space for intragranular ferrite growth. [ 20 ] Fig. 9 In-situ  observation images of Fe-0.2 pctC alloy heated to maximum holding conditions of ( a – c ) 1200 °C × 120 s, ( d – f ) 1400 °C × 120 s, and cooled at 70 °C/min

To verify the finding of the effect of PAGS on IGF formation,  in-situ  HT-CLSM observations were also performed on Fe-0.4 pctC steel under the same heating and cooling profiles. As shown in Figures  10 (a) through (c), samples were heated up and held at 1200 °C for 120 seconds, exhibiting the minimal microstructural evolution after cooling. This indicates the suppression of IGF nucleation. In contrast, the samples held isothermally at 1400 °C [Figures  10 (d) through (f)] showed GBF and IGF transformations starting at approximately 640 °C and 625 °C, and the finishing temperature is around 600 °C. These observations confirm that the coarse austenite grains can favor IGF nucleation and growth, which was consistent with findings in Fe-0.2 pctC alloy. Fig. 10 In-situ  observation of Fe-0.4 pctC alloy with different holding conditions of ( a – c ) 1200 °C × 120 s, and ( d – f ) 1400 °C × 120 s with a 70 °C/min cooling rate

Figure  11  shows the phase and inverse pole figure (IPF) color maps of Fe-0.4 pctC and Fe-0.2 pctC alloys under different cooling rates. The phase maps reflect the distribution of BCC (body-centered cubic) and FCC (face-centered cubic) phases, with grain boundaries indicated as white lines and the proportions of low-angle and high-angle grain boundaries labeled. In both alloys, the BCC phase dominates at cooling rates of 70 °C/min and 600 °C/min, but the grain morphology is finer at the faster cooling rate. The IPF color maps further reveal the grain arrangement characteristics. In the Fe-0.4 pctC alloy, the grain orientations are more uniform, and the grain size is larger with slow cooling. See Figure  11 (a-2). After rapid cooling, the orientation distribution becomes more diverse. See Figure  11 (b-2). This trend is more pronounced in the Fe-0.2 pctC alloy. Fig. 11 EBSD analysis of the investigated alloys: ( a-1 ,  b-1 ,  c-1 ,  d-1 ) phase maps, ( a-2 ,  b-2 ,  c-2 ,  d-2 ) inverse pole figure (IPF) color maps. Conditions: (a) Fe-0.4 pct C alloy at 1400 °C, cooled at 70 °C/min, (b) Fe-0.4 pctC alloy at 1400 °C, cooled at 600 °C/min, (c) Fe-0.2 pctC alloy at 1400 °C, cooled at 70 °C/min, (d) Fe-0.2 pctC alloy at 1400 °C, cooled at 600 °C/min

The histograms in Figure  12  show the variation in grain size. The Fe-0.4 pctC alloy, which was cooled at 70 °C/min, exhibits relatively coarse grains with a maximum size of 80.07  μ m and an average size of 44.51  μ m. See Figure  12 (a-1). When the cooling rate was increased to 600 °C/min, the maximum and average grain sizes decreased to 26.54 and 16.04  μ m, corresponding to reductions of about 67 and 64 pct, respectively. See Figure  12 (b-1). For the Fe-0.2 pctC alloy cooled at 70 °C/min, the maximum grain size is 256.22  μ m and the average size is 143.68  μ m. See Figure  12 (c-1). At 600 °C/min, the grain size decreases to 113.71  µ m and the average grain size decreases to 59.13  µ m, corresponding to reductions of about 56 and 59 pct, respectively. See Figure  12 (d-1). Fig. 12 Quantitative statistical analysis of the investigated steels: ( a-1 ,  b-1 ,  c-1 ,  d-1 ) grain size distribution, ( a-2 ,  b-2 ,  c-2 ,  d-2 ) grain boundary misorientation distribution. Conditions: (a) Fe-0.4 pctC alloy at 1400 °C, cooled at 70 °C/min, ( b ) Fe-0.4 pctC alloy at 1400 °C, cooled at 600 °C/min, ( c ) Fe-0.2 pctC alloy at 1400 °C, cooled at 70 °C/min, ( d ) Fe-0.2 pctC alloy at 1400 °C, cooled at 600 °C/min

IGF nucleates from intragranular inclusions with random orientations. This leads to an interlocked morphology within prior austenite grains. [ 40 ]  Increasing inclusion-induced IGF nucleation enhances impingement and increases the HAGB (high-angle grain boundaries, misorientation > 15 deg) fraction. [ 41 ]  The resulting HAGBs impede and deflect crack propagation, improving impact toughness. [ 42 ]  In the misorientation analysis of the Fe-0.4 pctC cooled at 70 °C/min, LAGBs (low-angle grain boundaries) account for 70.2 pct and HAGBs account for 29.8 pct. At 600 °C/min, the proportion of HAGBs increased to 61.7 pct, and the LAGBs proportion decreased to 38.3 pct. See Figure  12 (d-1). The Fe-0.2 pctC alloy shows a similar trend, with higher cooling rates promoting the formation of high-angle grain boundaries.

In summary, under conditions with larger PAGS, although a slower cooling rate can induce IGF nucleation and growth, increasing the cooling rate further refines the grains by inducing IGF formation and increases the proportion of high-angle grain boundaries. This is believed to be beneficial for the low-temperature toughness of the product. Song  et al. [ 43 ]  also reported that larger prior austenite grains and higher cooling rates promote IGF nucleation and increase its fraction. In contrast, finer grains tend to suppress IGF formation. These findings are consistent in both Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC alloys.

sections.heading: Effect of Cooling Rate on Nucleation and Growth of IGF
paragraphs: As shown in Section  B , IGF nucleation is obviously suppressed in the Fe-0.4 pctC alloy with a PAGS of about 33  µ m and a cooling rate of 70 °C/min. This leads to an IGF area fraction of only 0.92 pct. Under the conditions of such low PAGS, this section systematically examines the effects of higher cooling rates,  i.e.,  300 and 600 °C/min, on IGF nucleation behavior, growth kinetics, and final microstructure in the Fe-0.4 pctC isothermally held at 1200 °C for 120 seconds.  In-situ  HT-CLSM observation experiments reveal that the increased cooling rates can markedly influence nucleation behavior, transformation temperatures, and ultimately morphologies GBF and IGF.

According to Figure  13 , no obvious phase transformation was observed at a cooling rate of 70 °C/min. This confirms that IGF nucleation is suppressed by limited space within the small grain size. Increasing the cooling rate to 300 °C/min led to GBF nucleation at grain boundaries at 597 °C, followed by IGF nucleation at 564 °C from the inclusion surface. The finishing transformation could be observed at around 520 °C and a limited number of dispersed IGF are formed. For the 600 °C/min cooling rate, GBF nucleates at 576 °C and IGF at 556 °C, and the finishing temperature is around 516 °C. The final microstructure contains a significantly larger amount of IGF. Fig. 13 In-situ  observation images of HT-CLSM of Fe-0.4 pctC alloy heated at 1200 °C for 120 s under different cooling rates: ( a – c ) 70 °C/min, ( d – f ): 300 °C/min, ( g – i ): 600 °C/min

In addition to nucleation behavior, the cooling rate also significantly influences the growth kinetics of IGF. According to the comparative analysis of multiple IGF growth rate studies by Mu  et al. [ 4 ]  the growth of IGF is hindered by other grain boundaries or grains. This results in significant differences in the growth rates of individual ferrite phases, as illustrated in Figure  16 . Thus, the maximum IGF growth rate can be considered to represent the unimpeded growth rate, providing a more accurate reflection of the intrinsic growth kinetics. Fig. 16 Determination of the actual IGF growth rate

This study adopts the maximum IGF growth rate as the definitive value for the actual growth rate. IGF laths with relatively clear growth paths were randomly selected. Their lengths were measured from the HT-CLSM images using Image-J software. Figure  17  presents the measured data of the evolution of representative IGF lengths over time at different cooling rates. The measurement results indicate that at cooling rates of 70, 300, and 600 °C/min, the actual IGF growth rates are 1.34, 17.48, and 19.01  μ m/s, respectively. The increase in cooling rate elevates the degree of supercooling during phase transformation, significantly enhancing the nucleation driving force of IGF. [ 46 ]  This markedly increases its growth rate. This is attributed to enhanced inclusion-assisted nucleation associated with larger undercooling and accelerated growth kinetics within the studied cooling-rate window. Fig. 17 Increase of IGF lath length with time at different cooling rates: ( a ) 70 °C/min, ( b ) 300 °C/min, and ( c ) 600 °C/min

To characterize the final microstructure of specimens subjected to different processing conditions, EBSD analysis was conducted. Figure  18  presents typical phase maps (a-2 and b-2) and IPF maps of the Fe-0.2 pctC alloy. Both samples were heated at 1200 °C for 120 seconds, while the cooling rates for sample a and b were 70 and 600 °C/min, respectively. It can be observed that the BCC phase is the primary matrix, with a minor fraction of FCC structure also present. Fig. 18 EBSD analysis of the investigated Fe‑0.2 pctC alloy: ( a‑1 ,  b‑1 ) phase maps, ( a‑2 ,  b‑2 ) inverse pole figure maps. Conditions: (a) heated at 1200 °C for 120 s, cooled at 70 °C/min, (b) heated at 1200 °C for 120 s, cooled at 600 °C/min

Quantitative analysis of Figure  18  demonstrates that under conditions of small PAGS, increasing the cooling rate significantly refines microstructural characteristics. For the sample a cooled at 70 °C/min, the average grain size is 18.3  μ m, the d 50  value is 15.2  μ m, and the HAGB proportion is 45.3 pct. In contrast, for the sample b cooled at 600 °C/min, the average grain size decreases to 10.5  μ m, the d 50  value reduces to 8.7  μ m, and the HAGB fraction significantly increases to 58.6 pct. The HAGB density remains lower at 70 °C/min. When the prior austenite grains are relatively small, increasing the cooling rate promotes the formation of IGF in the final microstructure and increases the fraction of HAGB (Figure  19 ). Fig. 19 Quantitative analysis of the investigated alloys: ( a-1 ,  b-1 ) grain size distribution; ( a-2 ,  b-2 ) grain boundary misorientation angle distribution. Conditions: (a) Fe-0.2 pctC alloy, heated at 1200 °C for 120 s, cooled at 70 °C/min; (b) Fe-0.2 pct C alloy, heated at 1200 °C for 120 s, cooled at 600 °C/min

Table  V  summarizes the GBF and IGF phase transformation starting temperatures (T GBF,S  and T IGF,S ) for both alloys under the specified conditions. In both cases, the Fe-0.4 pctC alloy exhibits significantly lower GBF and IGF starting temperatures than those of Fe-0.2 pctC alloy. This is primarily because the carbon element can act as a strong austenite stabilizer, reducing the thermodynamic driving force for the  γ  to  α  transformation. To quantify this effect, the carbon content varied from 0.05 to 0.4 pct while keeping other elements constant in the calculations. As shown in Figure  20 , the driving force for IGF formation decreases markedly with increasing carbon content. The thermodynamic calculations confirm that the higher carbon content in the Fe-0.4 pctC alloy lowers the phase transformation driving force, requiring a greater undercooling to initiate IGF nucleation. Figure  21  is a concluding illustration that summarizes the synergistic effect of grain size and cooling rate on IGF nucleation and growth in steels with a wide range of carbon content,  i.e.,  from 0.2 to 0.4 pct in this work. The grain size is controlled by heating the steels to a maximum temperature of 1200 to 1400 °C and holding shortly ( i.e.,  120 s in this work). It was found that coarse-grain samples can favor IGF formation at a slow cooling condition, while fine grain sample requires a faster cooling rate to promote its formation. In addition, a higher cooling rate can promote the formation of high-angle grain boundaries of IGF, thereby optimizing the final microstructure to achieve a better toughness. This work utilizes two representative alloys compositions for a wide range of conventional carbon steels and provides microstructure design flexibility considering the general heat treatment conditions to control grain size and cooling rate. This work aims to apply the “oxide metallurgy” concept not only to optimizing the microstructure in CGHAZ of weldment (fine grain and fast-cooling rate) but also in a conventional casting condition (coarse-grain and slow cooling rate). sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In the current Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC alloys, the effective inclusions for inducing IGF nucleation are primarily TiN-contained complex inclusions. The inclusion sizes are mainly distributed in the range of 0.5 to 2.0  μ m, with approximately 60 pct of the inclusions concentrated within the size range of 0.5 to 1.0  μ m, which is beneficial for IGF nucleation. In both Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC alloys, increasing the maximum holding temperature can significantly increase the PAGS. Coarse grains reduce the energy barrier for both types of ferrite nucleation and provide more intragranular nucleation sites. Cooling rate and grain size hold a synergistic effect on IGF formation. Increased cooling rate can serve as the driving force to induce ferrite formation. For the case of coarse-grain, the slow cooling rate can lead to sufficient nucleation and growth of IGF, however the steel with fine grain requires a fast-cooling condition. The obtained findings are verified in both Fe-0.2 pctC and Fe-0.4 pctC alloys. Carbon is an interstitial element which could stabilize the austenite and decrease the thermodynamic driving force and inhibit both GBF and IGF formation. Specifically, IGF fraction as well as its formation temperature are observed to decrease with the increasing carbon content 0.2 to 0.4 pct in the current alloy series.
